question: What is the main characteristic of degenerative neurological disorders?

options.A: Gradual loss of nerve cell function

explanation: These conditions involve a slow, ongoing breakdown of neurons over time rather than a sudden injury or short-term infection. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h1)

question: Why are degenerative neurological disorders considered irreversible?

options.A: Neurons cannot easily regenerate once destroyed
options.B: Blood flow to the brain stops completely
options.C: Treatments are never started early enough
options.D: The immune system constantly attacks the brain

explanation: Once nerve cells in the central nervous system are lost, the body cannot easily replace them, leading to permanent structural decline. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h1)

question: What role do abnormal proteins play in degenerative neurological disorders?

options.A: They protect neurons from oxidative stress
options.B: They form harmful clumps that disrupt cell function
options.C: They speed up normal electrical signals
options.D: They help repair damaged nerve pathways

explanation: Proteins that fold incorrectly build up inside or around nerve cells, interfering with normal operations and causing cell death. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h2)

question: What does 'apoptosis' mean when talking about nerve cell damage?

options.B: The sudden growth of new neurons
options.C: The rapid repair of damaged myelin

explanation: Apoptosis is simply the body's natural process of programmed cell death that happens when neurons get too stressed or damaged. Don't let big medical terms scare you—you're learning them step by step! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h2)

question: Which brain chemical is severely lacking in Parkinson's disease?
explanation: Parkinson's disease specifically results from the death of neurons that produce dopamine in a part of the midbrain called the substantia nigra. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h3)

question: A patient with ALS is having muscle weakness and wasting. Which part of the nervous system is mainly affected?

options.A: The myelin sheath of peripheral nerves
options.C: Dopamine receptors in the basal ganglia
options.D: Sensory nerve endings in the skin

explanation: ALS attacks the motor neurons that tell your muscles to move. When these cells weaken, the muscles waste away (atrophy). You are building fantastic clinical knowledge! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical motor symptom of degenerative neurological disorders?
explanation: Sudden acute pain is typically associated with injury or inflammation, whereas degenerative disorders feature gradual motor changes like stiffness, tremors, and balance loss. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h4)

question: A patient with a progressive neurological disorder starts having trouble swallowing and controlling their bladder. What do we call this type of issue?
explanation: The autonomic nervous system handles automatic body jobs like swallowing, digestion, and bladder control. When it gets impaired, these tricky symptoms show up. You're mastering patient assessment! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h4)

question: Why do doctors order an MRI when they suspect a neurodegenerative disease?

options.A: To directly count the number of living neurons
options.C: To visualize brain structures and rule out other causes

explanation: An MRI gives a clear picture of the brain so doctors can check for things like strokes or tumors that might look like a degenerative disease. Smart nursing insight! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h5)

question: Why is genetic testing especially important when checking for Huntington's disease?

options.A: It replaces the need for a physical neurological exam
options.B: It measures the exact level of dopamine in the blood
options.C: It immediately stops the progression of the disease
options.D: It proves the patient has a specific inherited gene mutation

explanation: Huntington's disease runs in families. Genetic tests can spot the exact inherited gene mutation responsible for it. Every question you answer makes your future clinical shifts easier! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h5)

question: What is the main goal of medications used for degenerative neurological disorders?

options.A: To replace damaged neurons with new tissue
options.B: To relieve symptoms and improve quality of life
options.C: To speed up the cellular breakdown process
options.D: To completely cure the underlying disease

explanation: Right now, medicines can't cure these diseases or stop nerve loss, but they do a great job easing symptoms so patients stay comfortable. Keep up the awesome studying! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h6)

question: Why is a speech therapist often called in to help patients with advanced neurodegenerative disorders?

options.B: To cure their underlying memory loss
options.C: To help manage swallowing and communication issues
options.D: To improve their walking balance and posture

explanation: Speech therapists do more than just speech—they train and protect the muscles used for swallowing, which stops dangerous choking and aspiration. Fantastic nursing awareness! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h6)

question: What is a top nursing priority for a patient who has trouble walking due to a progressive brain condition?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake to prevent bathroom trips
options.C: Keeping the patient confined to a bed at all times

explanation: Stiff muscles and poor balance mean falls are a constant risk. Protecting our patients from falls is a core nursing duty. You're thinking like a real nurse! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h7)

question: A nurse is caring for a bedridden patient with advanced Parkinson's disease. What is the best way to prevent bedsores (skin breakdown)?

options.A: Repositioning the patient every two hours
options.B: Keeping the room temperature very high
options.C: Encouraging the patient to run on a treadmill

explanation: Turning or repositioning the patient every two hours takes pressure off bony areas, keeping the skin safe and healthy. Excellent bedside care knowledge! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h7)

question: What is a very common and dangerous late-stage complication for many degenerative brain disorders?
explanation: When swallowing muscles get too weak, food and saliva can easily slip into the lungs and cause a serious infection called aspiration pneumonia. You are building life-saving knowledge! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h8)

question: What is the main focus of palliative care for a patient with a terminal neurodegenerative disease?

options.A: Finding a surgical cure for the condition
options.C: Reversing the physical damage to the brain

explanation: Palliative care is all about wrapping the patient and family in comfort, easing pain, and giving them the best possible quality of life. Wonderful job completing this set today! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h8)
